text: Tiny just answered three plus four. Seven!
Yes! Right answer. Reward of one. Treat time!
Hmm. But was that actually good news?
What do you mean? Right is right.
Picture two questions. On an easy one, all eight of Tiny’s tries score one.
On a hard one, just one try out of eight scores one.
Oh. So the same one means nothing on the easy question... and it’s gold on the hard one!
Exactly. A score only means something next to the usual score. By the end of this video, you’ll know the trick that gets that usual score for free.
Groups and advantages. Episode one.
Here’s how a clever teacher does it. She asks the whole class the same question: seven plus five.
And collects eight answers. Twelve, thirteen, twelve, eleven, two, twelve, seventy-five, fourteen!
Three of them said twelve, the right answer. So the class average is three out of eight: about zero point three eight.
So nobody gets a mark out of ten. Just: better than the class, or worse?
Exactly. The three twelves beat the average, and the other five fall below it. That’s the whole idea of a group.
Last episode, we compared each answer with the usual score. But where does the usual score come from?
The older method, PPO, hires a critic: a second network that tries to predict the usual score.
A second network? How big?
Usually about as big as the model you’re training. Double the memory. And the critic can be wrong, too.
GRPO, from the DeepSeekMath paper in 2024, simply fires the critic.
Ha! And uses the class average instead.
Let’s do it properly. The same question, asked eight times.
The grader checks each one. Three right, five wrong.
Average: zero point three eight. That’s Tiny’s own success rate on this exact question, right now.
One more number: the spread, how far apart the scores are. Here, about zero point four eight.
Each answer’s advantage is its reward, minus the average, divided by the spread.
So the twelves get plus one point two nine... and the wrong ones, minus zero point seven seven.
Above zero: make that answer more likely. Below zero: less likely. And they always add up to zero.
Your turn. Two groups. In one, only one answer out of eight is right. In the other, four are right.
Which right answer gets the bigger push?
Pause, and have a guess.
Easy. A! Right is right. A treat’s a treat, so they get the same push.
Nice try, but no. It’s B. The lone right answer gets a much bigger push.
When something rare happens, the group notices.
Here’s the group with just one right answer.
Whoa, that twelve shoots right up! Plus two point six four!
And each wrong answer gets only a gentle push down, minus zero point three eight. Being wrong was normal here.
The rare success stands out. That’s exactly the answer we want more of.
Line them up and you can hear the logic.
A lone right answer: plus two point six four. A big deal.
A coin flip, four out of eight: plus one.
And if seven are right, the surprise is the one mistake. It gets the big push down: minus two point six four.
So the push is bigger when the result is more surprising.
But watch this. Nine plus eight, and every single answer is wrong.
Average zero. Spread zero. So every advantage is... zero?
Zero. This group teaches Tiny nothing at all. And if all eight were right? Same thing. Nothing.
Huh. That’s kind of honest, actually. If everyone’s wrong, nobody knows which way is better.
And at the start, that happens a lot. Tiny is guessing from nineteen possible answers.
With just two answers per group?
About nine groups in ten are all wrong. No signal at all.
With eight answers, about two in three. With sixteen, about four in ten.
So bigger groups go silent less often. Why not ask a hundred times?
Because every answer costs time. For a real model, writing those answers is the slowest part. Eight is a common default.
Quick recap.
Ask the same question several times, and the group’s average is the yardstick. No critic needed.
Each answer’s advantage says how much better or worse it did than its group.
And when every answer scores the same, nobody learns anything.
But here’s the catch. Remember that plus two point six four?
That’s a big push, on one lucky answer.
And what if we push it again? And again? Won’t Tiny end up saying twelve to everything?
It could. One big step can wreck what Tiny already knew. Next episode: the two safety brakes that stop it.
